name: Sodium hydroxide relaxer
lead: A sodium hydroxide relaxer, commonly called a lye relaxer, is a cream-based chemical hair straightener that uses sodium hydroxide as its active alkali to permanently loosen tight curls. Lye creams typically combine sodium hydroxide, usually at about 5 to 10 percent, with petroleum jelly, mineral oil and emulsifiers, and have a pH of roughly 10 to 14.[1] Relaxers act by breaking disulfide bonds in the hair shaft; the change applies only to treated hair and new growth emerges in its natural texture.[2]

It is used mainly on coarse, tightly coiled hair and has a long history among African American women and men.[2] Published research on relaxers has focused on health associations (fibroids, breast and uterine cancer) and on scalp and hair damage; these studies generally do not separate lye products from other relaxer types.[1]

paras: Sodium hydroxide raises the pH of the hair so that the internal bonds holding curls break, allowing the hair to be combed straight; no separate neutralising chemistry beyond rinsing and conditioning is described as necessary in the activation step.[1] Some products are labelled 'base', meaning a protective petroleum jelly layer is applied to the scalp first, while 'no base' products use lower lye concentrations.[1]

Garrett Augustus Morgan is reported to have developed an early straightening cream in 1909, reportedly by accident, and lye relaxers were sold from 1917.[1] The earlier straightening-comb tradition was popularised by Madam C. J. Walker in the early 1900s.[2]

Wikipedia reports that lye and no-lye relaxers can cause scalp burns, irritant or allergic dermatitis, brittleness and breakage, and that severe chemical burns can follow overexposure.[1] Broader concerns raised in the literature include kidney injury, effects on puberty and fertility, and cancer, though many of these relate to other ingredients such as phthalates or formaldehyde-releasing agents.[1][2]

No studies specific to sodium hydroxide relaxers were identified. Studies of relaxer use in general include a 2012 cohort of over 22,000 African American women that found an association with uterine fibroids, with no causal claim made; the NIH-AARP analysis of over 33,000 women, which reported that frequent users of hair straightening products had nearly double the uterine cancer risk; and reports linking relaxers to breast cancer. These studies did not analyse products by alkali type.[1][2] A questionnaire study of 90 women reported frizz, dandruff, hair loss and thinning among users.[1]

The US FDA does not pre-approve cosmetics, and a full ingredient list is not mandatory. In 2023 the FDA proposed banning formaldehyde as a relaxer ingredient, and lawsuits have been filed against manufacturers alleging failure to disclose risks.[1]

timeline.event: Garrett Morgan reportedly develops an early straightening cream.[1]
NIH reports an association between hair straightening products and uterine cancer.[2]
FDA proposes banning formaldehyde in relaxers.[1]

card.summary: The classic lye cream that permanently straightens tight curls; strong on straightening, with documented scalp-burn risk and broader health associations under study.
card.note: Can cause chemical burns and breakage; relaxer use is associated with health outcomes in observational studies.

quick.overview:
A sodium hydroxide relaxer is the traditional 'lye' cream used to permanently straighten very curly hair. It is applied to the hair, not the roots of new growth, which keeps its natural texture.

It is a long-established cosmetic product, sold since the early twentieth century.
quick.mechanism: The strongly alkaline sodium hydroxide breaks the disulfide bonds in the hair shaft so curls can be straightened.
quick.risks: Reported effects include scalp burns, dermatitis, dryness and breakage. Observational studies of relaxer use generally have linked it to fibroids and some cancers, though they do not distinguish lye from other types. Cosmetics are not pre-approved by the FDA.
